paragraphs: Learning rewards from human behavior means inferring what makes a sequence of decisions desirable. Demonstrations and preference feedback offer different evidence about that reward. This paper develops a common framework for both, motivated by robustness problems that can arise when reward learning depends on assumed models of human decisions or preferences.

The framework uses linear programming and works entirely with previously collected trajectories, without exploring an environment online. It estimates a set of feasible rewards through primal-dual optimality conditions: mathematical relationships connecting a linear optimization problem with its corresponding dual problem. The result is a collection of reward functions consistent with the framework’s constraints.

The authors provide an optimality guarantee and provable sample efficiency. They also incorporate human feedback, including comparisons between pairs of trajectories, while preserving computational tractability and sample efficiency. Analytical examples and numerical experiments suggest that the framework can outperform conventional maximum likelihood estimation. This is evidence of a possible advantage, rather than a claim that linear programming always produces better rewards.
icml-2024-a-unified-linear-programming-f.tldr: A linear programming framework learns feasible reward functions from offline demonstrations and feedback with optimality and sample-efficiency guarantees.

paragraphs: A neural network’s Jacobian describes how its outputs change when its inputs change. Penalizing this sensitivity adds another object to the training problem beyond the predictions themselves. This paper extends infinite-width neural network theory to study the network and its Jacobian together, providing a mathematical account of training with such a penalty.

The authors prove that, at initialization, a multilayer perceptron and its Jacobian jointly approach a Gaussian process as all hidden-layer widths grow without bound. They characterize this limiting process, describing the random behavior of both predictions and input sensitivities within one framework. The infinite-width setting is central to this result.

They also show that training with a Jacobian regularizer follows a linear first-order differential equation in that limit, governed by a variant of the Neural Tangent Kernel. Experiments demonstrate the relevance of these predictions to wide finite networks. Further empirical analysis of the associated kernel regression solution offers insight into Jacobian regularization, linking the limiting mathematics to behavior observed in networks of finite size.
icml-2024-an-infinite-width-analysis-on-.tldr: An infinite-width theory jointly describes neural network predictions, input sensitivities, and training with Jacobian regularization.

paragraphs: Language models can call external functions to obtain information or perform operations beyond their own capabilities. Coordinating those calls one at a time can introduce latency, expense, and errors. LLMCompiler addresses this orchestration problem by planning multiple calls and executing tasks in parallel, drawing inspiration from the organization of classical compilers.

The system separates orchestration into three components. A Function Calling Planner produces an execution plan, a Task Fetching Unit dispatches tasks, and an Executor runs them in parallel. This separation turns function calling into an explicitly organized workflow. The framework automatically generates an optimized orchestration and supports both open-source and closed-source language models.

Across benchmarks containing different function-calling patterns, the authors report consistent latency improvements, reaching a speedup of 3.7 times. They also report cost savings of up to 6.7 times and accuracy improvements of up to approximately 9% compared with ReAct. These are observed upper-end improvements across the evaluated tasks. The results suggest that organizing tool execution can improve efficiency and answer quality together.
icml-2024-an-llm-compiler-for-parallel-f.tldr: LLMCompiler plans and executes parallel function calls, reporting lower latency and cost and improved accuracy compared with ReAct.

paragraphs: Prediction sets express uncertainty by returning multiple plausible outcomes rather than one answer. Conditional coverage asks whether their reliability holds under particular input conditions. Full conditional guarantees for nontrivial sets are impossible in general, so researchers study relaxed versions. This paper asks whether learning uncertainty structure can improve those relaxed guarantees.

Partition Learning Conformal Prediction, or PLCP, learns uncertainty-guided features from calibration data. This differs from approaches that start with a predefined uncertainty structure. The framework uses alternating gradient descent and existing machine learning models, making the learned structure part of the procedure for constructing prediction sets rather than something fixed in advance.

The authors analyze PLCP theoretically and establish conditional guarantees for both finite and infinite sample sizes. Experiments across four real-world and synthetic datasets report better coverage and length performance than state-of-the-art methods in classification and regression. These findings support learning how uncertainty varies across inputs. They should be understood within the paper’s conditional-guarantee framework, which does not remove the general impossibility of unrestricted full conditional coverage.
icml-2024-conformal-prediction-with-lear.tldr: PLCP learns uncertainty-guided features from calibration data to improve prediction sets and provide conditional coverage guarantees.

paragraphs: Generating plausible molecules is different from reliably generating valuable candidates beyond the examples used for training. The paper focuses on this second challenge. Although diffusion models perform well at unconditional generation and guided generation within their training domain, directing them toward high-value regions outside that domain remains difficult.

Context-guided diffusion, or CGD, uses unlabeled data and smoothness constraints to improve the generalization of guided diffusion models. The method is designed as a simple, plug-and-play addition. Its central idea is to bring additional contextual information and smoothness requirements into the effort to guide generation beyond the training distribution.

The authors report substantial performance improvements across continuous, discrete, and graph-structured diffusion settings, with applications in drug discovery, materials science, and protein design. This range matters because the approach is demonstrated across several forms of generated data. The findings support context-guided diffusion as a way to improve out-of-distribution design in the evaluated settings, while reliable sampling of high-value candidates beyond training data remains the broader challenge motivating the work.
icml-2024-context-guided-diffusion-for-o.tldr: Context-guided diffusion uses unlabeled data and smoothness constraints to improve molecular and protein generation beyond the training distribution.

paragraphs: Training a neural network involves a nonconvex optimization problem, which complicates reasoning about how close a solution is to the best possible one. This paper studies two-layer ReLU networks trained with weight decay. It compares their optimization objective with a convex relaxation, a more tractable mathematical problem used to approximate the original.

For random training data, the authors bound the relative optimality gap by a factor of O(√log n), where n is the number of training examples. They use this result to obtain a polynomial-time algorithm that solves the original nonconvex problem up to a logarithmic factor. The guarantee concerns approximation, and the random-data setting is part of its stated scope.

The paper also shows that local gradient methods reach a point with low training loss with high probability under mild assumptions. The authors describe their result as an exponential improvement over existing results. Together, these findings connect tractable convex approximations with the success of local optimization, offering theoretical support for good training outcomes in the analyzed setting.
icml-2024-convex-relaxations-of-relu-neu.tldr: For random data, convex relaxations yield polynomial-time approximation guarantees for training weight-decayed two-layer ReLU networks.

paragraphs: Molecular generation often has to work with small datasets because collecting relevant molecules through experiments is expensive and slow. HI-Mol addresses this constraint by learning hierarchical information about molecules. Its motivation is that both broad patterns and finer distinctions matter when trying to capture a molecular distribution from few examples.

The method adapts textual inversion, an approach used for data-efficient image generation. Rather than representing the target distribution with a single level of token embeddings, HI-Mol learns embeddings at multiple levels. These represent coarse and fine information together. It then generates molecules by interpolating between the learned multi-level embeddings, using their combined structure to support generation.

The authors report strong data efficiency across extensive experiments. On QM9, HI-Mol outperforms the previous state-of-the-art method while using 50 times less training data. They also demonstrate that its generated molecules are useful for molecular property prediction when data is scarce. These findings support the value of hierarchical embeddings for both generation and a related prediction task in the evaluated low-data settings.
icml-2024-data-efficient-molecular-gener.tldr: HI-Mol learns hierarchical token embeddings to generate molecules efficiently, outperforming prior work on QM9 with 50 times less training data.

paragraphs: When data describes an outcome from several perspectives, useful information can lie in combinations of features. A synergistic interaction occurs when features provide more information together than separately. This paper focuses on identifying such combinations across multiple views, alongside feature subsets whose interactions are non-synergistic.

The authors formalize this selection problem using interaction information, an information-theoretic concept for describing relationships among variables. They introduce a deep learning method that searches for feature subsets with different interaction types. Because direct subset search is intractable, the method employs a Bernoulli relaxation to make the selection problem amenable to its learning procedure.

Experiments on synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real-world datasets show that the method discovers relevant feature subsets and closely matches ground truth in the reported evaluations. The authors also corroborate discovered features using medical and scientific literature. This provides support for the interpretive usefulness of the selected combinations: the method aims to reveal dependencies across views, rather than merely rank individual features by how informative they appear alone.
icml-2024-discovering-features-with-syne.tldr: An information-theoretic feature-selection method identifies combinations across multiple data views that become especially informative when considered together.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model to retain capabilities of a larger teacher, reducing the cost of using the model. For language models that generate sequences step by step, the paper identifies two challenges: the lack of a standardized training objective and the computational expense of incorporating outputs generated by the student.

DistiLLM addresses both through a two-part framework. First, it introduces a skew Kullback-Leibler divergence loss and uses its theoretical properties to guide distillation. This loss provides a way to compare teacher and student output distributions. Second, an adaptive off-policy approach improves the efficiency with which training uses student-generated outputs.

Student-generated outputs matter because they help address the mismatch between training and the conditions a student encounters when generating its own sequences. DistiLLM aims to retain this benefit with less computation. Extensive experiments, including instruction-following tasks, demonstrate high-performing students and speedups of up to 4.3 times compared with recent distillation methods. The reported gain concerns the evaluated distillation procedures, rather than a universal acceleration for all language-model training.
icml-2024-distillm-towards-streamlined-d.tldr: DistiLLM combines a skew divergence loss with efficient use of student-generated outputs, achieving distillation speedups of up to 4.3 times.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers information from a larger teacher network to a smaller student. Many approaches match individual feature representations or relationships between pairs of them. TopKD asks whether the broader organization of a network’s latent space also provides useful knowledge, particularly when that space has complex structure.

The method describes this global organization using persistence diagrams. These capture geometric characteristics such as distribution shape, connectivity, and structure at multiple scales. TopKD introduces a topology distillation loss to teach the student this information. The intended transfer therefore includes how representations are organized collectively, beyond the individual points or pairs emphasized by earlier methods.

Computing and transferring this information must also be practical. The authors use approximated persistence images of the diagrams to keep the transfer within reasonable computational time. Their experiments support the benefits of global topology as a source of knowledge and demonstrate the potential of TopKD. The findings make an empirical case for including broader latent-space structure in distillation, without claiming that topology is always the best information to transfer.
icml-2024-do-topological-characteristics.tldr: TopKD transfers global latent-space structure from teacher to student using a topology-based loss and computationally practical approximations.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning tries to infer a reward function from an expert’s demonstrations. The paper highlights two difficulties: learning can require many demonstrations, and a reward inferred from behavior in one environment may fail to handle even small changes in the environment’s dynamics. Collecting more data in that same setting does not necessarily resolve the latter problem.

The proposed framework gives the learner an active role in choosing where demonstrations occur. It repeatedly selects an environment and observes the expert acting there. Environment selection is adaptive, with the aim of identifying the reward function as quickly as possible. The information-gathering process therefore includes choosing the conditions under which expert behavior is observed.

Experiments show improvements in both sample efficiency and robustness, using exact as well as approximate inference. These findings support adaptive environment design as a useful part of reward learning. The approach depends on repeated interaction with an expert in learner-selected environments, making that interaction structure a central feature of how it obtains informative demonstrations.
icml-2024-environment-design-for-inverse.tldr: Adaptively choosing environments for expert demonstrations improves reward-learning sample efficiency and robustness in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Learning jointly from sound and images depends on recognizing their correspondence. Data augmentation can enrich training examples, but modifying audio or visual inputs can also disrupt that correspondence. EquiAV tackles this tension in self-supervised audio-visual contrastive learning, where the relationship between paired inputs provides a learning signal.

The framework brings equivariance into audio-visual learning: it accounts for how representations change under transformations. A shared attention-based transformation predictor supports this process. Features from several augmentations are then aggregated into a representative embedding, allowing multiple transformed versions to contribute to robust supervision instead of relying on a single augmented pairing.

The authors report that this aggregation introduces minimal computational overhead. Ablation studies and qualitative results support the effectiveness of the approach, and EquiAV outperforms previous work across several audio-visual benchmarks. The findings suggest that explicitly handling transformations can make augmentation more useful when learning across modalities. The practical contribution is a way to draw on diverse augmented features while addressing the correspondence problems that make audio-visual augmentation difficult.
icml-2024-equiav-leveraging-equivariance.tldr: EquiAV accounts for transformations and combines augmented features to improve audio-visual learning with minimal computational overhead.

paragraphs: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand how neural networks produce their predictions. One challenge is that networks trained on the same simple task can learn different algorithms, sometimes using several at once. This paper considers whether such variability limits the usefulness of examining internal representations and individual neurons.

The authors argue that high-dimensional networks can nevertheless learn useful low-dimensional representations of their training data. These representations can offer more than accurate predictions: studying them may reveal concepts that align closely with human domain knowledge. The claim is about the possibility of extracting meaningful understanding from a learned representation, even when the full network is complicated.

The paper develops this argument through a nuclear physics case study. By inspecting models trained to reproduce nuclear data, the authors extract nuclear physics concepts. This supports the view that interpretability can help researchers understand the problem a model has learned to solve. The case study illustrates that potential through agreement with established domain knowledge, rather than establishing that every network will contain equally accessible or scientifically useful concepts.
icml-2024-from-neurons-to-neutrons-a-cas.tldr: A nuclear physics case study shows how interpreting learned representations can recover meaningful scientific concepts from predictive neural networks.

paragraphs: Continual learning involves encountering tasks over time, and the semantic differences between successive tasks can vary considerably. Some changes are mild, while others are abrupt. The paper argues that fixed prompt-management strategies, designed around a uniform degree of change, struggle when a task sequence mixes both kinds of shifts.

AdaPromptCL responds by adapting how prompts are grouped. Its assign-and-refine mechanism manages prompt groups according to semantic similarity between tasks. Grouping is also continuously refined, allowing the organization to change as learning proceeds. This makes task relationships an ongoing part of prompt management instead of treating the initial grouping strategy as permanently appropriate.

Experiments report improvements of up to 21.3% over existing prompting methods, especially on benchmarks with diverse semantic shifts. The reported findings support adapting prompt organization to the variation actually present across tasks. The contribution is particularly relevant to sequences where one fixed assumption about task similarity is inadequate: the method aims to accommodate both closely related and sharply different tasks within the same continual-learning process.
icml-2024-one-size-fits-all-for-semantic.tldr: AdaPromptCL adaptively groups and refines prompts to handle continual-learning tasks with mixed mild and abrupt semantic shifts.

paragraphs: Transformer models learn representations of tabular data by using self-attention to combine information. That combination can also produce oversmoothing, where representations become too similar and lose useful distinctions. This paper shows that the problem affects Transformers for tables, extending a concern already identified in other uses of self-attention.

The authors propose a replacement self-attention layer built using matrix polynomials. Rather than introducing an entirely separate table-learning framework, they design the layer to take the place of the original attention component. The approach targets oversmoothing within existing models and is also presented as contributing to improved model scalability.

The evaluation equips three representative table-learning models with the proposed layer. In these experiments, the replacement mitigates oversmoothing and improves representation performance, with results exceeding state-of-the-art table representation methods. Testing it in several models supports the usefulness of changing this shared component. The findings connect the quality of learned table representations to how attention combines information, showing that a revised attention operation can help preserve useful distinctions in the evaluated systems.
icml-2024-polynomial-based-self-attentio.tldr: A matrix-polynomial attention layer reduces oversmoothing and improves representation learning in three evaluated tabular models.

paragraphs: Embedding layers turn tokens, such as words, into numerical vectors by looking them up in a table. Performing this step while keeping inputs encrypted is an important part of private machine learning. The paper addresses an efficiency gap in homomorphic-encryption implementations, where embedding layers have received less attention than other model components.

The authors develop an encrypted indicator function that enables precise table lookup using CKKS, an approximate homomorphic encryption scheme. Building on this function, they introduce CodedHELUT for encrypted embedding layers. Coded inputs improve efficiency and memory usage, making the representation of the lookup request part of the computational design.

The empirical analysis covers synthetic tables and large word-embedding models, including GloVe, GPT-2, and BERT embeddings. The method maintains 16-bit precision, with reported amortized evaluation times of 0.018–0.242 seconds for GloVe6B50d and 0.262–3.283 seconds for GPT-2 and BERT embedding layers. These results demonstrate a practical encrypted lookup component while preserving the confidentiality of input data through homomorphic computation.
icml-2024-privacy-preserving-embedding-v.tldr: CodedHELUT makes encrypted embedding lookup more efficient using coded inputs and a high-precision encrypted indicator function.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a difficult probability distribution using a more manageable family of distributions. Choosing that family affects both flexibility and computational cost. In black-box variational inference, full-rank covariance approximations scale poorly with problem dimension. This becomes especially important in hierarchical Bayesian models with local variables, where dimension grows with dataset size.

The paper studies structured variational families as a middle ground between mean-field and full-rank approximations. Its focus is on how the structure of the scale matrix affects iteration complexity. For the setting discussed, full-rank families lead to an explicit quadratic dependence, O(N²), on the number of data points N.

The authors prove that certain scale-matrix structures improve this dependence to O(N). This establishes a theoretical scaling advantage for the specified structures, rather than for every structured family. Experiments on large hierarchical models support the theoretical findings. The result makes the choice of approximation structure a concrete computational decision: it can change how the required number of iterations grows as the dataset expands.
icml-2024-provably-scalable-black-box-va.tldr: Certain structured variational families reduce BBVI’s dataset-size dependence in iteration complexity from quadratic to linear.

paragraphs: Policy optimization trains a decision-making strategy by adjusting it according to an objective. This paper studies an objective based on conditional value-at-risk, or CVaR, which emphasizes costly outcomes in the adverse tail. The challenge is to incorporate that risk-sensitive objective into policy-gradient methods ordinarily used for risk-neutral optimization.

The proposed predictive CVaR policy gradient changes how individual cost terms contribute to the gradient. Each term receives a weight proportional to its predicted contribution to the CVaR objective. A separate learning procedure estimates these weights. The prediction therefore influences how strongly a cost term shapes the update to the policy.

This reweighting is designed to integrate with existing risk-neutral policy-gradient algorithms using only small modifications. The authors provide both theoretical and empirical analyses supporting the method’s validity and effectiveness. Its significance lies in connecting a risk-sensitive objective to an established optimization workflow: the gradient is redirected through learned contribution weights, providing a route to CVaR-focused learning without requiring a wholly separate policy-optimization framework.
icml-2024-risk-sensitive-policy-optimiza.tldr: Predictive CVaR policy gradients adapt existing policy-gradient algorithms by weighting costs according to their predicted contribution to risk.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts models can increase their parameter count without a matching increase in computation. However, storing more experts still creates pressure to add GPUs. Uneven token assignments introduce another problem: some experts receive much more work than others, causing wasted computation or slow workers that hold up training.

ES-MoE addresses memory capacity and workload imbalance together. It stores expert parameters in host memory and processes experts through a pipeline that overlaps transfers between CPU and GPU with GPU computation. It also dynamically balances token loads across GPUs. These mechanisms target both the cost of moving expert parameters and the unequal distribution of work.

The authors validate the method on GPT-based MoE models, reporting faster training on a limited number of GPUs without degraded model performance. Compared with existing frameworks, they demonstrate 67 times better scalability and up to 17.5 times better throughput. These results support combining offloading, pipelining, and load balancing to expand feasible MoE training beyond GPU memory constraints in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-scaling-beyond-the-gpu-memory-.tldr: ES-MoE combines expert offloading, pipelined processing, and load balancing to scale MoE training beyond GPU memory limits.

paragraphs: Semantic image synthesis generates an image from a map of labels describing its contents. In practical use, those maps can contain mistakes, making robustness to noisy input important. This paper introduces a Stochastic Conditional Diffusion Model, or SCDM, whose forward and generation processes are designed specifically for synthesis with noisy labels.

Its central mechanism is Label Diffusion, which randomly perturbs semantic maps through a discrete diffusion process. As the timestep increases, noisy and clean versions of a map become more similar, eventually becoming identical at the final timestep. This convergence facilitates generating an image close to a clean image despite imperfections in the original labels.

The method also uses a class-wise noise schedule, allowing labels from different classes to undergo diffusion differently. Experiments and analyses on benchmark datasets demonstrate high-quality generated samples, including in a new setup that simulates human input errors. The findings support explicitly modeling uncertainty in the conditioning labels as part of the generation process when semantic maps may be imperfect.
icml-2024-stochastic-conditional-diffusi.tldr: SCDM diffuses semantic labels alongside its image-generation process to improve robustness to noisy input maps.

paragraphs: Flood forecasting depends on predicting river discharge at gauging stations. Data-driven systems often treat these locations separately, even when they belong to the same river network. This paper investigates whether explicitly representing connections between gauges helps forecasting, using graph neural networks to model discharge across a network of stations.

The authors compare different definitions of adjacency, examining how the choice of connections affects predictions. In their experiments, the model does not benefit from the river network’s topology, either across the whole network or within small subgraphs. Learned edge weights also fail to correlate with the static connection definitions and show no regular pattern.

The graph neural networks additionally struggle with sudden, narrow discharge spikes. Together, these findings challenge the expectation that a known physical network will necessarily improve a neural forecast. The authors suggest that the results may reflect a broader phenomenon in which graphical structure does not always help prediction. Their study motivates investigating the conditions under which structure is useful, rather than establishing that river topology is universally uninformative.
icml-2024-the-merit-of-river-network-top.tldr: The evaluated graph neural networks gain no forecasting benefit from river topology and struggle to predict sharp discharge spikes.

paragraphs: Subgraph representation learning assigns useful representations to parts of a larger graph. Specialized neural networks often perform this task directly on the full graph, requiring substantial memory and computation while facing difficulties with hierarchical subgraph structure. This paper changes the formulation by turning the subgraphs of interest into nodes of a new graph.

Subgraph-To-Node translation, or S2N, constructs that new graph through a coarse transformation of the supplied subgraphs. Simple graph neural networks can then learn on the resulting representation. The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that this approach captures local and global subgraph structure while reducing memory and computational costs compared with state-of-the-art models.

Graph coarsening also helps the method outperform baselines when the available set of subgraphs is small. Across eight benchmarks, fine-tuned models using S2N process 183–711 times more subgraph samples than state-of-the-art models while achieving better or similar performance. The results show how changing the unit represented by a graph node can improve efficiency without sacrificing predictive quality in the reported evaluations.
icml-2024-translating-subgraphs-to-nodes.tldr: S2N turns subgraphs into nodes of a new graph, enabling much more efficient representation learning with better or similar benchmark performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether wide and deep ReLU neural network classifiers approach the best achievable prediction accuracy as more data becomes available. It proves universal consistency for the classifiers under study. Consistency concerns their eventual statistical behavior, while the separate question of convergence rates asks how quickly improvement occurs with increasing data.

The authors also provide sufficient conditions on classes of probability measures under which neural network classifiers attain minimax-optimal convergence rates. Such rates describe the best achievable worst-case behavior for a specified class. The conditions are sufficient: the result establishes optimal rates when they hold, without claiming that those conditions are necessary.

The framework applies to a broad range of known function classes and extends beyond settings that impose explicit smoothness assumptions on the regression function. The abstract also identifies classifiers minimizing zero-one loss and exhibiting benign overfitting. Together, these results connect expressive ReLU architectures with statistical guarantees, including settings where fitting the training data closely can coexist with good generalization.
icml-2024-universal-consistency-of-wide-.tldr: The paper proves consistency for wide and deep ReLU classifiers and gives sufficient conditions for minimax-optimal convergence rates.

paragraphs: Information retrieval commonly uses separate models for finding candidate documents and ranking them. Retrieval benefits from independently computed embeddings, while ranking can use a cross-encoder to score a query and document together. USTAD asks whether one Transformer encoder can supply both forms of relevance information.

The proposed training approach produces a single network that works as a cross-encoder and also supplies factorized embeddings for dual-encoder retrieval. Empirically, this unified model is competitive with separate models for the two stages. USTAD also combines with an embedding-matching distillation method that improves the transfer from cross-encoder capabilities to dual-encoder students.

The distillation approach motivates asymmetric student architectures designed to align student and teacher embeddings while keeping online inference costs small. On standard benchmarks including MSMARCO, the resulting students use one-tenth of the trainable parameters while retaining 95–97% of teacher performance. The findings support both sharing a model across retrieval stages and using that model to train smaller students with strong retained performance in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-ustad-unified-single-model-tra.tldr: USTAD trains one encoder for retrieval and ranking and supports compact students that retain 95–97% of teacher performance on reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Pretrained image models are often judged by their performance across many downstream tasks. This requires real-world evaluation data and ties assessment to the selected tasks. The paper proposes using synthetic problems to evaluate representations in a task-agnostic way, with the aim of revealing capabilities that extend beyond a particular application.

The approach builds binary classification tasks using Gaussian mixtures. These synthetic tasks probe pretrained representations, and their robustness-accuracy behavior is compared with an idealized reference. The reference provides a basis for interpreting performance, while the synthetic construction reduces dependence on real-world datasets during representation evaluation.

Experiments with several pretrained image models find that this evaluation correlates with actual downstream linear-probing performance. It can also guide parameter choices for robust linear probing, improving the balance between robustness and accuracy. These findings support the usefulness of synthetic Gaussian benchmarks as informative probes of representation quality. The observed correlation connects the synthetic assessment to downstream behavior, without making the two evaluations interchangeable in every setting.
icml-2024-what-would-gauss-say-about-rep.tldr: Synthetic Gaussian classification tasks provide representation-quality assessments that correlate with downstream linear probing and help tune robustness-accuracy trade-offs.
